content.goal: Run the full ATLAS system end to end and read its trace.
content.why: The capstone proves the whole system works together: agentic RAG, a sub-agent, guardrails, approval, tracing, and reliability — one coherent agent. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 17-18.)
content.code:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    answer, trace = guarded_run(
        "Research our current project's deadline from my notes, "
        "then tell me how many days remain if today is March 1."
    )
    print(answer)
    print("TRACE:", trace.summary())
content.verify: ATLAS runs the multi-hop research through the sub-agent, stays grounded and cited, passes guardrails, records a full trace, and answers. Reading the trace, you can account for every step it took.

content.goal: Run the EXACT same build on your OTHER operating system.
content.why: Cross-platform is a first-class goal — the venv-based build runs on both Windows and Ubuntu 24.04 with only the activation command differing. (Learned across all build phases.)

commands.windows:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
python atlas.py
commands.ubuntu:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python3 atlas.py

content.verify: ATLAS produces the same behavior on the second OS. If you have both machines, confirm it there; if not, confirm the commands match what you have been using and that a requirements.txt captures your dependencies.
content.troubleshoot: If a dependency is missing on the second OS, run `pip freeze > requirements.txt` on the working machine and install from it on the other. That file is your portable dependency contract.

content.why: A pinned dependency list makes the build reproducible on any machine — the same discipline as pinning versions in any project. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 17, section 17.6.)
content.verify: requirements.txt lists openai, python-dotenv, pydantic, fastapi, uvicorn, and any others you used, with pinned versions. Anyone can now recreate your environment.

content.goal: Run the production-readiness checklist against ATLAS.
content.why: Before calling an agent "ready," you should be able to say yes across reliability, cost/latency, safety/observability, and quality/operations. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 17, section 17.8.)
content.code:
# Tick each honestly for ATLAS:
# RELIABILITY: retries+backoff? timeouts? provider fallback? step/output caps? idempotent actions?
# COST/LATENCY: right-sized model? tight prompts? concise tool results? tokens tracked?
# SAFETY/OBSERVABILITY: input/output/action guardrails? injection defense + least privilege?
#                       human approval on dangerous tools? tracing on every run? no secrets in logs?
# QUALITY/OPERATIONS: an eval suite with a threshold gate? .env secrets (never in code)?
content.verify: You can answer YES (or "consciously deferred, and here's why") to each item. ATLAS meets the core of a production-readiness bar.

content.goal: Write a short README describing ATLAS with the six-question universal recipe.
content.why: Any agent is defined by six questions — goal, tools, knowledge, architecture, guardrails, interface. Writing them down is how you understand and hand off any agent. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 18, section 18.1.)
content.code:
# README.md — answer the six questions for ATLAS:
# 1. GOAL: research/ops assistant that answers from my documents and runs safe tools.
# 2. TOOLS: search_docs, word_count, reverse_text, research (sub-agent), delete_file (gated).
# 3. KNOWLEDGE: my docs via RAG (chunk -> embed -> retrieve -> grounded answer + citation).
# 4. ARCHITECTURE: single ReAct agent + a research sub-agent (supervisor topology).
# 5. GUARDRAILS: input/output/action layers; injection defense; human approval on delete.
# 6. INTERFACE: a FastAPI /ask endpoint (and the CLI).
content.verify: A README.md exists answering all six questions for ATLAS. You can now describe — and someone else can understand — exactly what your agent is and does.
